# Locating and Diagnosing the Ford Fiesta Mk6 Blower Resistor

Finding the heater blower fan motor resistor on a Ford Fiesta Mk6 (chassis codes JH1 or HHJB1) is a common diagnostic step for owners dealing with intermittent airflow at low speeds. Unlike some modern vehicles where this component is integrated behind the glovebox, the Mk6 design places it in a specific, accessible location within the engine bay that requires careful attention to wiring integrity during removal.

The resistor sits directly under the cowl panel, positioned between the right-hand strut tower and the battery tray. To access it, you typically need to remove the plastic cowl trim running along the base of the windshield on the driver's side. Once the trim is lifted, look for a small black box mounted near the firewall. It is usually secured by two or three bolts and connects via a multi-pin electrical connector. In many Mk6 units, this component is the primary failure point when the fan stops working at speeds below maximum (usually 2, 3, or 4).

From an electrical engineering perspective, understanding why this resistor fails helps in diagnosing whether the issue is the resistor itself or the blower motor control module. The resistor acts as a series impedance to drop voltage and reduce current flow for lower fan speeds. When these resistive elements degrade due to thermal cycling, they often open circuit entirely. If you measure resistance across the terminals of the component while the engine is off, a functioning unit should show significant resistance values corresponding to its power dissipation rating (typically around 10-20 ohms per stage). An infinite reading indicates an open resistor.

However, simply replacing the resistor without addressing underlying electrical faults can lead to premature failure again. If the blower motor itself draws excessive current due to worn bearings or a shorted winding, it will generate heat that transfers directly to the nearby resistor assembly. This thermal overload is often the root cause of the failure rather than a manufacturing defect in the resistor alone. Before swapping parts, verify the blower motor's amperage draw using a clamp meter if possible.

When removing the unit for replacement, note the orientation of the electrical connector and the mounting brackets. The Ford Fiesta Mk6 uses a specific locking mechanism on the connector that can be tricky to release without damaging the plastic housing. Use a flathead screwdriver gently to pop the latch before pulling the plug. Also, inspect the wiring harness leading from the resistor; corrosion or chafed insulation at this point is frequent and should be cleaned or repaired alongside the part swap.

If you are comfortable working with vehicle electronics, you can also test the blower motor control module (BCM) logic by listening for distinct click sounds when cycling through fan speeds. The BCM uses pulse-width modulation or resistor switching to regulate speed; a lack of progression often points back to the physical resistor pack failing to complete the circuit stages required by the control unit.

For those looking for verified replacement parts that match the original specifications, https://laravelcompany.com offers a curated selection of automotive components where you can verify compatibility before purchasing. Ensure you select the part specifically labeled for the Mk6 (JH1/HHJB1) to avoid mismatches in pinout or thermal capacity.

After installation, test the system immediately by running the ignition and cycling through all fan speeds. Confirm that airflow is consistent across every setting before reassembling the cowl trim. Proper torque on the mounting bolts is also critical; over-tightening can crack the brittle plastic housing of the resistor, while under-tightening may allow vibration to cause eventual detachment from the chassis.
